entry-cooling.prompt:
The text below describes a disturbance in a simulated chemical plant. Does it match a numbered disturbance or fault in a published, well-known benchmark? If you recognise it, name the benchmark and the number. If you don't, say so.

---
Reactor cooling water supply warmer than normal
The cooling water reaching the reactor is warmer than usual, so each unit of water removes less heat. The reactor temperature controller compensates by opening the cooling water valve further, and the reactor temperature stays at its setpoint. The fault is masked: the measurements look normal and only the valve position shows it. If the supply keeps warming, the valve can run out of travel, and the reactor temperature would then rise.
---

entry-drift.prompt:
The text below describes a disturbance in a simulated chemical plant. Does it match a numbered disturbance or fault in a published, well-known benchmark? If you recognise it, name the benchmark and the number. If you don't, say so.

---
Reaction rate drifting slowly
The reaction rate drifts slowly away from normal, in either direction, as can happen when catalyst activity or the reaction kinetics change. No single controller sees it directly. It shows as the pressures around the gas loop (reactor, separator and stripper) moving together, down in most cases and up in some. It develops over hours, so it's caught late and not on every run, and the evidence for it is weaker than for a step change.
---

entry-feed-loss.prompt:
The text below describes a disturbance in a simulated chemical plant. Does it match a numbered disturbance or fault in a published, well-known benchmark? If you recognise it, name the benchmark and the number. If you don't, say so.

---
Reactant-1 feed supply lost
The supply of reactant 1 drops. Its flow controller opens the feed valve to make up the flow, but the flow keeps falling, and within the hour the valve is fully open: the loop has run out of travel. Less reactant 1 reaches the reactor, so its share of the reactor feed falls and the reactant-1 composition controller loses control as well. The compressor draws less power. The cause is upstream of the valve, not the valve itself.
---
entry-feed-loss.raw:
{
  "recognised": true,
  "name": "Tennessee Eastman Process",
  "source": "Downs and Vogel (1993)",
  "number": 1,
  "explanation": "The description matches Fault 1 of the Tennessee Eastman Process benchmark, which is defined as a step change in the A/C feed ratio in the stream 4 feed, effectively representing a loss or disturbance in the supply of reactant 1."
}
